column1: How many round trips before the first request byte on a cold TLS 1.3 connection?
column2: Two -- one for the TCP handshake, one for TLS 1.3. TLS 1.2 needs three total. QUIC merges transport and crypto into one, and resumption with 0-RTT can reach zero for safe methods.
column3: frontend web-foundations DNS TLS HTTP latency

column1: Why does the initial TCP congestion window matter to first paint?
column2: A fresh connection may only send about 10 segments (~14 KB) before waiting for acknowledgements, doubling each RTT. Anything critical above ~14 KB costs additional round trips of pure transfer.
column3: frontend web-foundations DNS TLS HTTP latency

column1: Difference between `dns-prefetch`, `preconnect` and `preload`?
column2: `dns-prefetch` resolves the name only. `preconnect` does DNS + TCP + TLS and holds a socket. `preload` actually fetches a specific resource and requires an `as` attribute to set priority and the `Accept` header.
column3: frontend web-foundations DNS TLS HTTP latency

column1: Why is 0-RTT early data unsafe for `POST`?
column2: The early-data flight is replayable -- an on-path attacker can resend it and the server has no handshake freshness context to reject it. Safe for idempotent `GET`; mutations need either 1-RTT or server-side idempotency keys.
column3: frontend web-foundations DNS TLS HTTP latency

column1: What is Anycast and what does it break?
column2: One IP address advertised from many physical sites, with BGP routing each client to the nearest. It gives global low-latency from a single address, but it also means "the IP is up" says nothing about whether a specific site is healthy.
column3: frontend web-foundations DNS TLS HTTP latency

column1: Which DNS cache ignores your record TTL?
column2: The browser's. Chrome pins entries to roughly 60 seconds regardless of TTL, so DNS changes alone cannot be relied on for fast failover -- you need health-checked Anycast or a load balancer behind a stable address.
column3: frontend web-foundations DNS TLS HTTP latency

column1: What is the mobile radio promotion tax?
column2: On cellular an idle radio must be promoted to connected before any packet is sent -- typically 100-500 ms on LTE. It precedes your first RTT, never appears in server metrics, and is the main reason lab TTFB understates real mobile TTFB.
column3: frontend web-foundations DNS TLS HTTP latency

column1: Where is the HTTP protocol version actually chosen?
column2: In ALPN, carried inside the TLS ClientHello. The client offers `h2`, `http/1.1` (and advertises `h3` via `Alt-Svc` or DNS HTTPS records) and the server picks, so negotiation costs no extra round trip.
column3: frontend web-foundations DNS TLS HTTP latency

column1: Which two CSS properties can be animated without main-thread work?
column2: `transform` and `opacity`, on an element that has its own compositor layer. The compositor thread applies them while assembling the frame, so they stay smooth even when JavaScript is blocking. `filter` is also GPU-accelerated but is fill-rate heavy.
column3: frontend browser-rendering rendering main-thread reflow compositing

column1: What is a forced synchronous layout?
column2: Reading a geometric property (`offsetWidth`, `getBoundingClientRect()`, `getComputedStyle()`, `scrollTop`) after a style write. The browser must flush pending changes and run layout immediately to give a correct answer. In a loop it becomes layout thrashing -- one layout per iteration.
column3: frontend browser-rendering rendering main-thread reflow compositing

column1: Difference between `display: none` and `visibility: hidden` in the pipeline?
column2: `display: none` removes the node from the render tree, so it costs no layout or paint and occupies no space. `visibility: hidden` keeps it in the render tree -- it is laid out and takes up space, it is just not painted.
column3: frontend browser-rendering rendering main-thread reflow compositing

column1: Why is 50 ms the long-task threshold?
column2: The RAIL model puts 100 ms as the ceiling for an interaction to feel instantaneous. A task must stay under 50 ms so that even if input arrives just as it starts, the browser has ~50 ms left to dispatch and respond within budget.
column3: frontend browser-rendering rendering main-thread reflow compositing

column1: What does `{ passive: true }` actually promise?
column2: That your handler will not call `preventDefault()`. Without it the browser must run your `touchstart`/`wheel` handler before it knows whether to scroll, putting your JavaScript on the scroll critical path. With it, scrolling proceeds on the compositor immediately.
column3: frontend browser-rendering rendering main-thread reflow compositing

column1: What does `content-visibility: auto` do and what does it break?
column2: Skips style, layout and paint for off-screen elements until they approach the viewport. It breaks intrinsic sizing -- the element reports zero height -- so scroll height jumps and anchor links misfire unless you supply `contain-intrinsic-size`.
column3: frontend browser-rendering rendering main-thread reflow compositing

column1: Why is `will-change: transform` in a stylesheet usually a mistake?
column2: It permanently promotes every matching element to its own compositor layer, and each layer costs GPU memory proportional to its pixel area. On a list of hundreds of items this causes worse jank than it prevents. Set it in JS immediately before the animation and clear it on completion.
column3: frontend browser-rendering rendering main-thread reflow compositing

column1: Why does `setTimeout(fn, 0)` yield worse than `scheduler.yield()`?
column2: `setTimeout` queues a new macrotask behind everything already pending, so your continuation can be starved. `scheduler.yield()` returns a prioritised continuation that resumes ahead of other pending tasks, giving you responsiveness without losing throughput.
column3: frontend browser-rendering rendering main-thread reflow compositing

column1: What can a Web Worker not do, and what is the cost of using one?
column2: No DOM access and no layout APIs -- it is for pure computation. The cost is structured-clone serialisation on `postMessage`, which is significant for large objects; transferable `ArrayBuffer`s avoid the copy where the data format allows.
column3: frontend browser-rendering rendering main-thread reflow compositing

column1: Safe vs idempotent -- what is the difference?
column2: Safe means read-only, no intended state change (`GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`). Idempotent means N identical requests leave the same state as one. `DELETE` and `PUT` are idempotent but not safe. `POST` is neither; `PATCH` is not guaranteed idempotent.
column3: frontend http-and-networking HTTP QUIC idempotency retries

column1: Why is `PATCH` not idempotent?
column2: A patch body can express a relative change -- increment a counter, append to a list -- and applying it twice compounds. An absolute-value patch happens to be idempotent, but the method makes no such promise, so no proxy or gateway may retry it.
column3: frontend http-and-networking HTTP QUIC idempotency retries

column1: How does an idempotency key work, including the edge cases?
column2: Client sends a unique key per logical operation. Server claims the key *before* doing work; a repeat of a completed key replays the stored response, a repeat while in flight returns `409`, and the same key with a different body returns `422` because that is a client bug, not a retry.
column3: frontend http-and-networking HTTP QUIC idempotency retries

column1: Does HTTP/2 solve head-of-line blocking?
column2: Only at the application layer. TCP still delivers one ordered byte stream, so one lost packet stalls every multiplexed stream on that connection. Above roughly 2% loss a single HTTP/2 connection can be worse than six HTTP/1.1 ones. HTTP/3 over QUIC fixes it with per-stream loss recovery.
column3: frontend http-and-networking HTTP QUIC idempotency retries

column1: What is connection coalescing?
column2: If two hostnames resolve to the same IP and are covered by the same certificate, an HTTP/2 browser reuses one connection for both. It is why domain sharding became an anti-pattern -- extra hostnames now cost handshakes and cold congestion windows instead of buying parallelism.
column3: frontend http-and-networking HTTP QUIC idempotency retries

column1: What makes a CORS request "simple", and why does it rarely matter?
column2: `GET`/`HEAD`/`POST`, no custom headers, and `Content-Type` limited to form-urlencoded, multipart, or text/plain. `application/json` is excluded, so nearly every modern API call triggers an `OPTIONS` preflight -- a full extra round trip unless `Access-Control-Max-Age` is set.
column3: frontend http-and-networking HTTP QUIC idempotency retries

column1: Why does `Vary: Origin` matter on CORS responses?
column2: Without it a shared cache stores one origin's `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` value and serves it to requests from other origins, so the API appears to fail intermittently for some tenants. Combined with credentialed requests -- which forbid `*` -- it is a correctness requirement, not a tuning knob.
column3: frontend http-and-networking HTTP QUIC idempotency retries

column1: `412` vs `428` -- when do you use each?
column2: `412 Precondition Failed` answers a conditional write whose `If-Match` ETag no longer matches, preventing a lost update. `428 Precondition Required` rejects a write that arrived with *no* precondition at all, which is how you make blind overwrites impossible by policy.
column3: frontend http-and-networking HTTP QUIC idempotency retries

column1: Why did server push lose to `103 Early Hints`?
column2: The server cannot see the client cache, so push wasted bandwidth on assets the browser already had and competed with the critical path. Early Hints sends `Link: rel=preload` during server think time and lets the browser, which knows its own cache, decide whether to fetch.
column3: frontend http-and-networking HTTP QUIC idempotency retries

column1: Difference between `max-age` and `s-maxage`?
column2: `max-age` governs private caches (the browser). `s-maxage` governs shared caches (the CDN) and overrides `max-age` for them. Splitting them lets you cache HTML at the edge for speed while keeping browser TTL at zero for control.
column3: frontend cdn-and-edge CDN caching edge security

column1: What does `stale-while-revalidate` buy you?
column2: The user gets an instant response from the stale copy while the edge refreshes in the background. TTL expiry stops being a latency spike paid for by a real user.
column3: frontend cdn-and-edge CDN caching edge security

column1: What is an origin shield?
column2: A designated mid-tier cache that all edge PoPs fetch through. Without it, a miss can mean hundreds of PoPs hitting origin for the same object at once.
column3: frontend cdn-and-edge CDN caching edge security

column1: Why is `Vary: User-Agent` an anti-pattern?
column2: There are effectively unbounded UA strings, so each one becomes its own cache key. Your hit rate approaches zero and the origin sees near-full traffic.
column3: frontend cdn-and-edge CDN caching edge security

column1: Why should you never delete old hashed chunks on deploy?
column2: During a rollout users hold cached HTML referencing the previous build. Deleting those chunks gives them a white screen. Keep N-1 and N-2 live.
column3: frontend cdn-and-edge CDN caching edge security

column1: Preferred order of cache invalidation strategies?
column2: 1) Change the URL (content hashing) — instant and free. 2) Short `s-maxage` plus revalidation. 3) Explicit purge, which is rate-limited and eventually consistent, so never your rollback plan.
column3: frontend cdn-and-edge CDN caching edge security

column1: Which cache layer can you never invalidate?
column2: The HTTP browser cache. Once a response is stored with a `max-age`, it lives on the user's disk for that duration and no purge, deploy or API reaches it. The only recovery is serving from a different URL -- which is why content-hashed filenames exist.
column3: frontend caching-layers caching invalidation stampede

column1: What is a cache stampede and what are the three defences?
column2: When a hot key expires, every concurrent request misses at once and all hit the origin for the same value. Defences: request collapsing (single-flight lock so one recomputes), TTL jitter so keys do not expire together, and early probabilistic recompute or serve-stale-while-revalidating so nobody meets a cold key.
column3: frontend caching-layers caching invalidation stampede

column1: Why does adding Redis shards not fix a hot key?
column2: Cluster mode maps a key to a slot by hashing the key, so one key always lives on one node regardless of cluster size. You must either spread the value across N suffixed keys or prevent the reads reaching Redis at all with a very short in-process cache.
column3: frontend caching-layers caching invalidation stampede

column1: Cache-aside vs write-back -- what is the real difference?
column2: Cache-aside populates on miss and writes go to the database, so a cache failure means slow, not lost. Write-back acknowledges the write from the cache and flushes asynchronously, so writes are fast but unflushed data is permanently lost if the cache dies. Acceptable for counters and metrics, never for orders.
column3: frontend caching-layers caching invalidation stampede

column1: Why delete a cache key on write rather than update it?
column2: Updating races with an in-flight read that already holds the old row: the slow reader writes its stale value after your update, with a fresh TTL, leaving a silent inconsistency that never resolves. Deleting shrinks the window to the gap before the next read, which repopulates from current state.
column3: frontend caching-layers caching invalidation stampede

column1: What does a version prefix in a cache key buy you?
column2: `product:v3:42` means a schema change is deployed by bumping the prefix. Every old-shape entry is abandoned atomically with no purge and no window where clients receive two different shapes; the orphans simply expire.
column3: frontend caching-layers caching invalidation stampede

column1: What is negative caching and why is the TTL shorter?
column2: Storing a "not found" sentinel so repeated lookups of a non-existent ID do not pass through to the database -- the defence against enumeration and broken retry loops. The TTL is shorter (say 30 s vs 300 s) because not-found becoming found is a far likelier transition than the reverse.
column3: frontend caching-layers caching invalidation stampede

column1: How do you calculate the staleness a user can actually observe?
column2: Roughly the sum of the TTLs along the path, not the minimum -- each layer can be populated from an already-stale layer beneath it. Allocate freshness as a budget across layers, and make TTLs shorten as you move outward toward the user.
column3: frontend caching-layers caching invalidation stampede

column1: Why is a very high hit rate a risk as well as a win?
column2: It hides how the origin behaves under real load. A 96% hit rate means the database has never seen 25x its current read volume, so a cache outage or cold start is an untested capacity event. Find out deliberately with a cold-start game day rather than during an incident.
column3: frontend caching-layers caching invalidation stampede

column1: Why can SSR make INP worse than CSR?
column2: SSR paints a complete-looking page before the bundle has hydrated, so for hundreds of milliseconds it looks interactive and queues input instead of responding. CSR shows a skeleton that honestly signals "not ready". LCP improves while TBT and INP regress, which is invisible if you only track LCP.
column3: frontend rendering-strategies SSR SSG streaming hydration

column1: Roughly what does JavaScript cost to parse and compile on a mid-tier phone?
column2: About 1 ms per KB before any of your code executes, plus execution and reconciliation on top. A 500 KB bundle is therefore ~500 ms of parse/compile alone, and a mid-tier Android is 4-6x slower than a developer laptop on single-threaded JS.
column3: frontend rendering-strategies SSR SSG streaming hydration

column1: Lazy hydration vs partial hydration -- what is the difference?
column2: Lazy (progressive) hydration defers when the work happens; the same JavaScript is still shipped and eventually executed. Partial hydration (islands, RSC server components) means some components never ship JavaScript at all. Only the second one reduces the total bill.
column3: frontend rendering-strategies SSR SSG streaming hydration

column1: What does streaming SSR decouple TTFB from?
column2: Your slowest data dependency. The shell flushes in tens of milliseconds so the browser can start fetching CSS and fonts, and each `Suspense` boundary streams in as its query resolves, rather than the whole document waiting on the slowest query.
column3: frontend rendering-strategies SSR SSG streaming hydration

column1: What is locked once the first chunk of a streamed response flushes?
column2: The status code and all response headers. Auth checks, 404 decisions, redirects and `Set-Cookie` must be resolved before the shell goes out; anything failing after the flush must render an error inside its boundary instead of returning a 500.
column3: frontend rendering-strategies SSR SSG streaming hydration

column1: Why is streamed content an SEO risk despite Googlebot rendering JavaScript?
column2: Googlebot generally handles it, but social-preview scrapers (Slack, LinkedIn, Twitter) and many non-Google crawlers take only the initial HTML. Title, meta description, Open Graph tags, canonical URL, JSON-LD and primary copy must therefore live in the shell.
column3: frontend rendering-strategies SSR SSG streaming hydration

column1: How do you estimate SSR capacity?
column2: `renderToString` blocks the Node event loop, so throughput is roughly cores divided by render time. At 60 ms per render a core sustains ~16 renders/second, meaning 5,000 rps needs on the order of 300 cores before headroom, GC pauses and p99 render time.
column3: frontend rendering-strategies SSR SSG streaming hydration

column1: What causes a hydration mismatch and what does it cost?
column2: Any non-deterministic render -- `Date.now()`, `Math.random()`, locale or timezone formatting, `typeof window` branches. React discards the server HTML and re-renders on the client, so you paid the SSR compute and delivered a CSR experience, often with a visible flash.
column3: frontend rendering-strategies SSR SSG streaming hydration

column1: What is the right strategy for a page that is 98% shareable and 2% personalised?
column2: Split the response. Cache the shareable majority aggressively (SSG/ISR with `s-maxage`), and fetch or edge-inject the personalised fragment separately, so one cache policy does not have to serve both. Making the whole page per-request sacrifices cacheability for 2% of the pixels.
column3: frontend rendering-strategies SSR SSG streaming hydration

column1: What problem does a BFF actually solve?
column2: An ownership problem. Screens need data joined across domain services, and a BFF lets the client team do that joining in a service it owns -- on 0.5 ms internal links rather than 200 ms client ones -- without negotiating a backend roadmap slot or reshaping a domain API for one view.
column3: frontend api-and-bff REST GraphQL BFF contracts

column1: What must never live in a BFF?
column2: Business rules, its own primary database, cross-client shared logic, long-running work, and any server-side consumers. The test: if two clients could disagree about the answer, it is domain logic and belongs one layer down.
column3: frontend api-and-bff REST GraphQL BFF contracts

column1: What is the GraphQL N+1 problem and its fix?
column2: A nested field resolver runs once per parent item, so 50 posts requesting an author means 51 queries. DataLoader batches all loads made within one event-loop tick into a single `WHERE id IN (...)` and caches per request. Without it a GraphQL API will saturate its database well below expected traffic.
column3: frontend api-and-bff REST GraphQL BFF contracts

column1: Why does GraphQL break HTTP caching?
column2: Every query is a `POST` to a single `/graphql` URL, and every HTTP cache keys on URL plus method. Browser cache, service worker, CDN and reverse proxies all stop working at once. Persisted queries sent as `GET /graphql?id=<hash>` restore a cacheable URL.
column3: frontend api-and-bff REST GraphQL BFF contracts

column1: What do persisted queries give you beyond caching?
column2: A closed allowlist. Clients register queries at build time and send only a hash, so an attacker cannot author a query at all -- which addresses the complexity-based denial of service more completely than depth or cost limits alone.
column3: frontend api-and-bff REST GraphQL BFF contracts

column1: Offset vs cursor pagination -- the two real problems with offset?
column2: Correctness and cost. Concurrent inserts or deletes shift items across page boundaries, so users see duplicates or miss rows. And `OFFSET 100000` makes the database scan and discard 100,000 rows, so deep pages degrade linearly. Keyset cursors on `(sort_key, id)` are stable and O(limit) at any depth.
column3: frontend api-and-bff REST GraphQL BFF contracts

column1: What three fields make an error contract operationally useful?
column2: A stable machine-readable `code` (clients must never branch on message text), an explicit `retryable` flag so the client does not infer it from a status code, and a `traceId` that appears in your logs so a support ticket becomes a query rather than an investigation.
column3: frontend api-and-bff REST GraphQL BFF contracts

column1: What does consumer-driven contract testing add over an OpenAPI schema?
column2: It tests the fields consumers actually *use*, not the fields you *declare*. Each consumer publishes its expectations and the provider CI verifies all of them before deploy, so "does this change break anyone" becomes a build result instead of a changelog nobody read.
column3: frontend api-and-bff REST GraphQL BFF contracts

column1: When is tRPC the wrong choice?
column2: As soon as you have a consumer you cannot deploy in lockstep with, or one that is not TypeScript. There is no language-agnostic schema artefact and no versioning story by design, so a Swift client, a Kotlin client or a partner integration needs OpenAPI, GraphQL SDL or protobuf instead.
column3: frontend api-and-bff REST GraphQL BFF contracts

column1: What is the one test that separates server state from client state?
column2: Can another tab, another user, or another device change this value? If yes, you hold a copy of someone else's truth -- that is a cache, and it needs a staleness policy, refetch triggers and invalidation on mutation, not a slot in a global store.
column3: frontend state-management state react-query URL-state cache

column1: Why did server-state libraries replace most of Redux?
column2: Because most of what teams put in a global store was a local copy of server data -- a cache. Redux gave no staleness, invalidation or request lifecycle, so every endpoint grew hand-written loading and error flags. React Query and friends are caches with an invalidation model, and adopting one typically empties 70-80% of a legacy store.
column3: frontend state-management state react-query URL-state cache

column1: `staleTime` vs `gcTime` -- what is the difference?
column2: `staleTime` is how long a value is considered fresh, during which a new mount serves from cache with no request. `gcTime` is how long an *unused* value is retained before eviction, which is what makes back navigation instant. Conflating them is the most common misconfiguration.
column3: frontend state-management state react-query URL-state cache

column1: What are the three parts of a correct optimistic update?
column2: Snapshot the previous value in `onMutate` (and cancel in-flight refetches), restore that exact snapshot in `onError`, and invalidate in `onSettled` so the server reconciles regardless of outcome. Plus a user-visible message on rollback -- a silent revert is indistinguishable from success.
column3: frontend state-management state react-query URL-state cache

column1: When should state live in the URL?
column2: When a user could reasonably expect a copied link to reproduce the view: filters, search text, sort, page, active tab, open detail panel. You get sharing, refresh survival, and back/forward undo for free. The costs are validating user-editable input and using `replaceState` for high-frequency changes.
column3: frontend state-management state react-query URL-state cache

column1: Why is storing derived state a bug factory?
column2: It creates two facts that can disagree with nothing enforcing that they agree, so any code path that forgets to recompute produces a silently wrong UI. Compute at render; `useMemo` caches the computation without creating a second source of truth.
column3: frontend state-management state react-query URL-state cache

column1: What problem does normalisation solve, and when is it not worth it?
column2: The same entity appearing in a list, a detail and a search response means three copies that drift, so editing one leaves the others stale. Normalising stores entities once by ID with references elsewhere. Not worth it for dashboards of independent read-only widgets -- real complexity for a consistency problem you do not have.
column3: frontend state-management state react-query URL-state cache

column1: Why do global stores rot?
column2: Adding a key costs nothing and any component can read or write any value, so the store only grows and eventually nobody can answer "who writes this" or "what breaks if I delete it". Counter with small domain-scoped stores, server data kept out, and exposed actions instead of raw setters.
column3: frontend state-management state react-query URL-state cache

column1: What goes wrong when a form is initialised from server data?
column2: The form forks the data, so a refetch on window refocus can overwrite in-progress edits and the user's typing silently reverts. Disable refocus refetching while dirty, and send `If-Match` with the loaded ETag on submit so a concurrent change returns `412` rather than a silent last-write-wins overwrite.
column3: frontend state-management state react-query URL-state cache

column1: Is a re-render the same as a DOM update?
column2: No. The render phase calls your components and diffs the result; if the output is unchanged, the commit phase does nothing. Rendering 200 components that produce identical trees costs the function calls and the diff -- often under a millisecond -- and zero DOM work. Target expensive renders, not all renders.
column3: frontend react-at-scale React performance architecture

column1: What happens when the element type at a position changes?
column2: React unmounts the entire subtree and remounts it, destroying all state within it. This is why conditionally swapping a wrapper component around the same children clears form inputs, focus and scroll position.
column3: frontend react-at-scale React performance architecture

column1: Why does `React.memo` fail to stop rerenders from context?
column2: Because `useContext` subscribes the component directly to the provider rather than receiving a prop, so the memo comparison is not on that path. React also compares the whole context value by reference and has no field-level granularity.
column3: frontend react-at-scale React performance architecture

column1: When is `useCallback` load-bearing, and when is `React.memo` worse than nothing?
column2: `useCallback` earns its cost when the function goes to a `React.memo` child (otherwise the memo can never hit) or into another hook's dependency array (otherwise the effect re-runs every render, a correctness issue). `React.memo` is actively harmful with an inline object or array prop: the shallow comparison runs every parent render and always fails, so you pay it and re-render anyway while believing the component is memoised.
column3: frontend react-at-scale React performance architecture

column1: What does `useTransition` actually change?
column2: It marks an update non-urgent so React keeps urgent input responsive and can interrupt and restart the expensive render. It makes rendering interruptible, not faster or parallel -- and it cannot interrupt inside a single component's render, so one large synchronous computation is unaffected.
column3: frontend react-at-scale React performance architecture

column1: What are the real costs of virtualisation?
column2: In-page search cannot find unrendered rows; accessibility needs correct `aria-rowcount`/`aria-rowindex` since the DOM no longer reflects the list; variable-height rows need a measurement cache, which is where most bugs live; and `scrollIntoView` to an arbitrary row needs explicit support.
column3: frontend react-at-scale React performance architecture

column1: Why do index keys cause bugs rather than just slowness?
column2: React matches siblings by key, so with index keys the instance and its local state stay with the *position* while the props describe a different item. A checked checkbox, an input value or focus follows position through a sort -- a silent correctness bug with no warning.
column3: frontend react-at-scale React performance architecture

column1: What is the test for whether a component belongs in the shared design system?
column2: Used by three or more domains *and* its API has stopped changing. Promoting a still-evolving component makes every future change a coordinated migration across the whole application.
column3: frontend react-at-scale React performance architecture

column1: Why do barrel files undermine code splitting?
column2: `export * from ...` pulls the whole module graph into anything that imports one symbol, so a heavy dependency lands in every chunk and route splitting delivers little. Whether tree-shaking rescues you depends on side-effect analysis you are not checking -- so use deep imports and verify against the actual bundle report.
column3: frontend react-at-scale React performance architecture

column1: What do microfrontends actually buy you?
column2: Independent deployment. A team ships without waiting on another team's build, tests or release train. Not performance, not smaller bundles, not simplicity -- those are costs you pay for the autonomy.
column3: frontend microfrontends MFE org-design contracts

column1: Why does duplicate React break context silently?
column2: A context is an object identity created by one React instance. A provider from copy A and a consumer from copy B never match, so the consumer gets the `createContext` default value with no error thrown.
column3: frontend microfrontends MFE org-design contracts

column1: Which packages must be singletons in a shared scope?
column2: Anything holding module-level mutable state or relying on identity: `react`, `react-dom`, the router, the styling runtime, and the query client. Pure leaf utilities can duplicate cheaply.
column3: frontend microfrontends MFE org-design contracts

column1: Best-to-worst cross-microfrontend communication?
column2: URL/query state, then the server plus cache invalidation, then a shell-provided service, then namespaced custom DOM events. Direct imports between features are effectively never right.
column3: frontend microfrontends MFE org-design contracts

column1: How do you stop design-token drift across remotes?
column2: Ship tokens as CSS custom properties from the shell so components read `var(--ds-space-3)` instead of importing a number. Token changes then propagate on shell deploy regardless of bundled component versions.
column3: frontend microfrontends MFE org-design contracts

column1: What is the honest default instead of microfrontends?
column2: A modular monolith: one deployable, enforced module boundaries, code owners per directory, affected-only CI. You get ownership clarity while keeping a compile-time contract.
column3: frontend microfrontends MFE org-design contracts

column1: What conditions justify a real runtime split?
column2: Roughly eight or more teams shipping to one URL, a heterogeneous stack being strangled incrementally, or a compliance/trust boundary that forbids sharing a runtime.
column3: frontend microfrontends MFE org-design contracts

column1: Why are iframes sometimes the right microfrontend?
column2: They are the only option with a separate JS realm and origin, so a crash or a hostile script is contained. When you host untrusted or third-party code, that isolation beats bundle efficiency.
column3: frontend microfrontends MFE org-design contracts

column1: What does `remoteEntry.js` contain?
column2: A small manifest-plus-loader: what the remote exposes, what it can contribute to the shared scope, and an `init` function the host calls with the scope. It is the deploy pointer, so it must be short-TTL and revalidated, never immutable.
column3: frontend module-federation Module-Federation webpack versioning

column1: How does shared-scope version resolution choose a copy?
column2: Among all registered candidates satisfying the requesting side's `requiredVersion` range, the highest semver version wins, and an already-instantiated copy is reused. The host has no inherent priority.
column3: frontend module-federation Module-Federation webpack versioning

column1: Difference between `singleton` and `strictVersion`?
column2: `singleton: true` guarantees one instance in the realm and only warns on a version mismatch. `strictVersion: true` makes an unsatisfiable range throw at resolution time instead of silently falling back.
column3: frontend module-federation Module-Federation webpack versioning

column1: Why does `eager: true` exist, and what does it cost?
column2: It inlines a shared copy into the initial chunk so synchronous entry code can use it, avoiding the "not available for eager consumption" error. The cost is losing that package's negotiability -- prefer an async `bootstrap` import instead.
column3: frontend module-federation Module-Federation webpack versioning

column1: Why must remote URLs come from a runtime manifest?
column2: Hardcoded URLs in webpack config mean rolling back a remote requires rebuilding and redeploying the host, destroying deploy independence. A short-TTL manifest makes rollback an atomic pointer flip.
column3: frontend module-federation Module-Federation webpack versioning

column1: What does a React error boundary fail to catch here?
column2: Failed `remoteEntry.js` requests, chunk-load errors, rejected dynamic imports, and errors thrown while a module body evaluates. You need a `try/catch` with a timeout around the import as well as the boundary.
column3: frontend module-federation Module-Federation webpack versioning

column1: What is the N-1/N/N+1 problem?
column2: Production runs a combination of independently deployed versions, including browsers holding old shell HTML. The tested set is a list; the live set is a product. Survive it with additive-only contract changes, retained old chunks, and a mount-time contract check.
column3: frontend module-federation Module-Federation webpack versioning

column1: How do Import Maps dedupe dependencies?
column2: By URL identity -- every module importing the bare specifier `react` resolves to the same URL, so the browser evaluates it once. Simple and standards-based, but there is one entry per specifier per document, so no semver negotiation.
column3: frontend module-federation Module-Federation webpack versioning

column1: Why is `publicPath: "auto"` required in a remote?
column2: Without it, the remote's lazy chunk URLs resolve against the host's origin and path and 404. `auto` derives the base URL from the location of the running `remoteEntry.js`.
column3: frontend module-federation Module-Federation webpack versioning

column1: What are the three token layers and who references which?
column2: Primitives are raw values and are referenced only by the token package. Semantic tokens express intent and are the only layer product code and components may use. Component tokens let one component be retuned without touching the semantic layer.
column3: frontend design-systems design-system platform migration

column1: Why ship tokens as CSS custom properties rather than only a JS object?
column2: Because a component reading `var(--color-semantic-action-primary)` picks up a token change from a stylesheet update even if it was bundled months ago by another team. Tokens leave the JS dependency graph, so version skew stops being visible.
column3: frontend design-systems design-system platform migration

column1: Why is changing a default prop value a major version?
column2: Nothing fails to compile, so behaviour changes silently across every call site at once. Type-visible breaks announce themselves; silent default changes are found by users.
column3: frontend design-systems design-system platform migration

column1: Who owns the migration for a design-system breaking change?
column2: The team that made the change. That means writing the codemod and opening pull requests against every consuming repository -- not publishing a migration guide and a Slack message.
column3: frontend design-systems design-system platform migration

column1: What does `axe-core` catch and what does it miss?
column2: It catches contrast failures, missing accessible names, invalid ARIA and bad roles -- roughly a third of WCAG criteria. It misses focus order, whether announcements make sense, custom widget semantics, and focus return on modal close.
column3: frontend design-systems design-system platform migration

column1: Which governance model is the usual steady state, and what does it require?
column2: Federated: product engineers contribute, the platform team owns review, API standards and release. It requires a scaffold command, a written API checklist, and a real review-time commitment, or teams fork.
column3: frontend design-systems design-system platform migration

column1: Two adoption metrics worth a dashboard?
column2: Component adoption rate -- library instances over all rendered interactive elements from a static scan -- and local reimplementation rate. A rising reimplementation rate means your path costs more than going around you.
column3: frontend design-systems design-system platform migration

column1: When should a design system say no to a component?
column2: When there is one consumer and no visible second use case. That is a product component; promote it to the library when a second team needs it.
column3: frontend design-systems design-system platform migration

column1: What belongs on the non-visual paved road?
column2: Auth with token refresh, generated API clients, one telemetry SDK, shared build and deploy pipelines, a typed feature-flag client, and migration tooling: codemods, usage scanners and bot-authored upgrade pull requests.
column3: frontend design-systems design-system platform migration

column1: When is SSE the better choice than WebSocket?
column2: When traffic is one-way server-to-client and text: notifications, live logs, LLM token streams. You get automatic reconnection with `Last-Event-ID` replay for free, provided you have HTTP/2 end to end.
column3: frontend realtime-frontend WebSocket SSE realtime presence

column1: Why does SSE need HTTP/2?
column2: On HTTP/1.1 browsers allow six connections per origin and each SSE stream holds one for its lifetime, so a few tabs starve your normal API calls. HTTP/2 multiplexes streams on one connection, raising the practical limit to around 100.
column3: frontend realtime-frontend WebSocket SSE realtime presence

column1: What is full jitter and why not fixed-delay-plus-random?
column2: Full jitter picks a uniform random delay in [0, min(cap, base × 2^n)). Adding a small random offset to a fixed delay leaves the fleet clumped, so each retry wave still arrives together and re-saturates the service.
column3: frontend realtime-frontend WebSocket SSE realtime presence

column1: What is a resume token for?
column2: So a reconnecting client can say `since=lastSeq` and receive only the gap. Without it every reconnect costs a full snapshot, and a mass reconnect after a gateway restart becomes a bigger outage than the restart.
column3: frontend realtime-frontend WebSocket SSE realtime presence

column1: Why prefer facts over deltas in realtime messages?
column2: Delivery is at-least-once, so replays happen. Applying `unread = 3, version 118` twice is a no-op; applying `increment unread` twice permanently corrupts state with no path back to correct.
column3: frontend realtime-frontend WebSocket SSE realtime presence

column1: Why must presence be lease-based?
column2: Browsers do not reliably announce departure -- no `beforeunload` on a crash, force-quit or OS tab discard. So online means "renewed a TTL recently"; expire after 2-3 missed heartbeats or you accumulate ghosts forever.
column3: frontend realtime-frontend WebSocket SSE realtime presence

column1: Both directions of WebSocket backpressure?
column2: Server side: cap the per-connection send queue and disconnect with a resync code, or slow clients OOM the gateway. Client side: check `ws.bufferedAmount`, coalesce to one message per frame, and drop stale intermediate states.
column3: frontend realtime-frontend WebSocket SSE realtime presence

column1: How do you authenticate a WebSocket without headers?
column2: Mint a single-use ticket valid for about 30 seconds over authenticated HTTP and exchange it at handshake, so the credential in the URL and access logs is nearly worthless. Then renew over the connection with an `auth.renew` message.
column3: frontend realtime-frontend WebSocket SSE realtime presence

column1: Why do connections drop exactly every 60 seconds?
column2: A default idle timeout -- AWS ALB and nginx `proxy_read_timeout` are both 60 s. Heartbeat inside the window *and* raise the timeout; a cluster of close code 1006 is the diagnostic signal.
column3: frontend realtime-frontend WebSocket SSE realtime presence

column1: What is the outbox pattern?
column2: Apply the mutation to the local store and append an intent record to an outbox queue in one atomic transaction, then have a background loop drain the queue to the server with retries, backoff and error classification.
column3: frontend offline-and-sync offline IndexedDB outbox sync

column1: Why must the local write and outbox append share a transaction?
column2: Otherwise a crash between them leaves the UI showing a change that will never be sent -- silent data loss that is effectively unreproducible in development.
column3: frontend offline-and-sync offline IndexedDB outbox sync

column1: Why generate entity ids on the client?
column2: Creates become idempotent by construction, the local record never needs its id rewritten, and records created offline can already reference their parents without temporary ids and a rewrite pass.
column3: frontend offline-and-sync offline IndexedDB outbox sync

column1: What exact failure does `Idempotency-Key` protect against?
column2: The server committing the mutation and the response being lost. The client cannot distinguish that from a request that never arrived, so it retries; the key lets the server replay the stored result instead of re-executing.
column3: frontend offline-and-sync offline IndexedDB outbox sync

column1: Why never detect conflicts with client timestamps?
column2: Client clocks are routinely minutes off and can be set deliberately, so timestamp-based last-write-wins hands the race to whoever has the most skewed clock. Use server-assigned versions with `If-Match`.
column3: frontend offline-and-sync offline IndexedDB outbox sync

column1: When should a conflict be shown to the user?
column2: Only when both sides changed the same field of content the user authored. Different fields should merge, and prompting on every version mismatch just trains people to dismiss the dialog.
column3: frontend offline-and-sync offline IndexedDB outbox sync

column1: Why does a new service worker not take effect on reload?
column2: It installs and waits until every page controlled by the old worker is closed; a reload keeps the old worker alive. You must detect the waiting worker and call `skipWaiting` plus a reload, ideally with user consent.
column3: frontend offline-and-sync offline IndexedDB outbox sync

column1: What does `navigator.storage.persist()` do?
column2: Requests the persistent storage bucket so your origin is exempt from ordinary eviction. It can be denied based on engagement signals, so check the returned value -- especially on Safari, which clears script-writable storage after seven days of non-use.
column3: frontend offline-and-sync offline IndexedDB outbox sync

column1: Why does a sync change feed need tombstones?
column2: A client cannot infer deletion from absence, so deletions must be explicit events. Tombstones need a retention window, and a client with a cursor older than that window must be forced into a full resync.
column3: frontend offline-and-sync offline IndexedDB outbox sync

column1: Why does full-document last-write-wins lose edits?
column2: Each client sends a complete state built from what it last saw, so the later write asserts values for text the other user changed. One person's edit is overwritten with no error. Sending operations rather than states is what makes both preservable.
column3: frontend collaborative-editing CRDT OT collaboration

column1: What does Operational Transformation do?
column2: A central server rewrites an incoming operation against every operation committed since its base revision -- adjusting indices so intent survives -- then applies it. Clients mirror the transform for concurrent remote operations.
column3: frontend collaborative-editing CRDT OT collaboration

column1: Why is OT risky to implement yourself?
column2: You need a transform function for every ordered pair of operation types, so the matrix grows quadratically, each entry must satisfy transformation property 1, and a single wrong entry diverges only under specific concurrent timing. Several published algorithms shipped incorrect.
column3: frontend collaborative-editing CRDT OT collaboration

column1: How does a sequence CRDT avoid index-based positions?
column2: Every element gets a globally unique immutable id -- client id plus counter -- and inserts are expressed relative to a neighbour's id. Deletes leave tombstones, because removing an element would invalidate operations referencing it.
column3: frontend collaborative-editing CRDT OT collaboration

column1: Name four CRDT families and their use.
column2: LWW-Register for scalar fields where one value must win; PN-Counter for increments that must all count; OR-Set for tags and collaborator lists; sequence CRDTs such as RGA or YATA for text and lists.
column3: frontend collaborative-editing CRDT OT collaboration

column1: What do CRDTs not solve?
column2: Intent -- convergence is not meaning; authorisation -- the merge function rejects nothing; garbage collection -- tombstones grow monotonically; rich-text semantics across concurrent structural edits; and per-user undo.
column3: frontend collaborative-editing CRDT OT collaboration

column1: Why server-authoritative rather than peer-to-peer for a CRDT document?
column2: You need one enforceable authorisation point, durable storage when nobody is online, an audit trail, and debuggability. Peer-to-peer additionally brings NAT traversal, TURN relays and N² mesh growth. Use peer-to-peer for awareness only.
column3: frontend collaborative-editing CRDT OT collaboration

column1: What problem do snapshots solve?
column2: Two. Load time, since append-only update logs otherwise replay the document's entire history. And garbage collection, since a snapshot defines a horizon past which clients must reload rather than merge, which makes tombstone compaction safe.
column3: frontend collaborative-editing CRDT OT collaboration

column1: Why must undo be scoped by origin?
column2: Users expect ctrl-Z to revert their own last change, not the document's. Without origin tracking you undo whatever a collaborator just typed, which users correctly report as data loss.
column3: frontend collaborative-editing CRDT OT collaboration

column1: What are the Core Web Vitals thresholds, and at what percentile?
column2: LCP ≤ 2.5 s, CLS ≤ 0.1, INP ≤ 200 ms, all evaluated at the 75th percentile of page loads. p75 means one in four users can be worse and you still pass, which is why segmenting by device and geography matters more than the aggregate.
column3: frontend web-performance performance Core-Web-Vitals budgets RUM

column1: Why is INP harder than the FID it replaced in March 2024?
column2: FID measured only the input delay of the first interaction -- essentially queueing time -- so a page could pass while every interaction took a second to show a result. INP measures input to next paint for approximately the worst interaction, so it includes the handler and the rendering that follows.
column3: frontend web-performance performance Core-Web-Vitals budgets RUM

column1: What are the three parts of INP, and why does the split matter?
column2: Input delay (waiting for a free main thread), processing time (your handler), presentation delay (rendering the frame). If most of it is input delay, the handler is irrelevant and you need to find the long task blocking the thread -- usually hydration or a third-party script.
column3: frontend web-performance performance Core-Web-Vitals budgets RUM

column1: What does LCP decompose into, and which slice is usually largest?
column2: TTFB, resource load delay, resource load duration, and element render delay. Load *delay* is often the biggest -- the image was discovered late because it was referenced from CSS, injected by JavaScript, or lazy-loaded. That is a preload and `fetchpriority` fix, not a compression fix.
column3: frontend web-performance performance Core-Web-Vitals budgets RUM

column1: Name four reasons lab and field data disagree.
column2: Device distribution (real traffic spans a 5x CPU range), cache state (lab is always cold), network reality (packet loss and the 100-500 ms mobile radio promotion), and interaction (lab tools never click, so INP is unmeasurable and TBT is only a proxy). Plus geography and unfiltered bot traffic.
column3: frontend web-performance performance Core-Web-Vitals budgets RUM

column1: What is the most common LCP bug in the wild?
column2: A lazy-loaded hero image. `loading="lazy"` tells the browser to deliberately defer the most important resource on the page, adding hundreds of milliseconds. Use `loading="eager"`, `fetchpriority="high"` and a `preload` for anything that could be the LCP element.
column3: frontend web-performance performance Core-Web-Vitals budgets RUM

column1: FOIT vs FOUT -- which do you choose and how do you mitigate it?
column2: `font-display: block` gives FOIT, up to 3 s of invisible text which can delay LCP entirely. `font-display: swap` gives FOUT, immediate fallback text with a shift on swap. Choose swap, then remove the shift with `size-adjust`, `ascent-override` and `descent-override` on a fallback `@font-face`.
column3: frontend web-performance performance Core-Web-Vitals budgets RUM

column1: Why is a single Lighthouse run a bad CI gate?
column2: Variance is high enough to produce false failures, and a flaky gate gets disabled within a month. Take the median of about five runs, keep deterministic bundle-size checks as the first line on every PR, and provide a named override path so the gate is not deleted during an incident.
column3: frontend web-performance performance Core-Web-Vitals budgets RUM

column1: How do you make a credible business case for performance work?
column2: Cite published figures with their source and audience (Vodafone +8% sales from a 31% LCP improvement; Deloitte +8.4% retail conversion per 0.1 s) as evidence the mechanism is real, then segment your own funnel by metric bucket while naming the confounders, then run a holdback -- 90% treated, 10% on the old path -- for a causal number.
column3: frontend web-performance performance Core-Web-Vitals budgets RUM

column1: Why is XSS the highest-priority frontend vulnerability?
column2: Injected script runs as your origin, so it reads non-`HttpOnly` cookies and storage, reads the DOM including typed input, and issues fully authenticated requests. Every other frontend control is downstream of not having it.
column3: frontend frontend-security XSS CSP CSRF supply-chain

column1: What is DOM-based XSS?
column2: Your own JavaScript reads an attacker-influenced value -- a query parameter, a fragment, a `postMessage` -- and writes it to a dangerous sink like `innerHTML` or a `javascript:` URL. The server is never involved, so server-side filtering cannot help.
column3: frontend frontend-security XSS CSP CSRF supply-chain

column1: Why nonce plus `strict-dynamic` instead of a host allowlist?
column2: Allowlisting a host trusts every endpoint on it, and JSONP callbacks or open redirects on allowlisted domains let an attacker get code served from a trusted origin. Nonces trust specific script instances, and `strict-dynamic` makes browsers ignore host allowlists.
column3: frontend frontend-security XSS CSP CSRF supply-chain

column1: What does Trusted Types change?
column2: With `require-trusted-types-for 'script'`, dangerous sinks reject plain strings and accept only objects from a registered policy. The review surface collapses from every sink usage to a handful of policies.
column3: frontend frontend-security XSS CSP CSRF supply-chain

column1: Difference between `SameSite=Lax` and `Strict`?
column2: `Lax` sends the cookie on same-site requests and on top-level cross-site `GET` navigations, blocking cross-site `POST`. `Strict` withholds it even on a top-level navigation, so users arriving from an email link appear logged out.
column3: frontend frontend-security XSS CSP CSRF supply-chain

column1: Why is `SameSite=Lax` insufficient on its own?
column2: It is same-*site*, not same-*origin*. A compromised subdomain such as `blog.acme.com` is the same site as `app.acme.com` and can issue requests carrying your cookie. Add a double-submit or synchroniser token and an `Origin` check.
column3: frontend frontend-security XSS CSP CSRF supply-chain

column1: The honest difference between `localStorage` and `HttpOnly` for tokens?
column2: Exfiltration. With XSS an attacker can make requests either way, but a `localStorage` token can be sent to their server and replayed off-device for its full lifetime. An `HttpOnly` cookie cannot leave the browser, confining them to the live page.
column3: frontend frontend-security XSS CSP CSRF supply-chain

column1: What does PKCE protect against, and what does it not?
column2: It stops an intercepted authorisation code from being exchanged, since the attacker lacks the `code_verifier` behind the SHA-256 challenge. It does not cover CSRF on the redirect itself -- that is still the `state` parameter's job.
column3: frontend frontend-security XSS CSP CSRF supply-chain

column1: What is dependency confusion?
column2: If an internal package name is unregistered publicly, an attacker publishes it to the public registry and build systems configured with both may prefer it, executing their code in your pipeline. Fix it by mapping your scope to the internal registry in `.npmrc`.
column3: frontend frontend-security XSS CSP CSRF supply-chain

column1: Why report metrics on `visibilitychange` rather than `unload`?
column2: `unload` is unreliable and never fires when a mobile tab is discarded, while `visibilitychange` to hidden always does. `sendBeacon` there survives page teardown, and CLS and INP are only final at page hide anyway.
column3: frontend frontend-observability observability RUM errors tracing

column1: What does web-vitals attribution add?
column2: It decomposes a metric into actionable parts -- which element was the LCP candidate, and how the time split between time-to-first-byte, resource load delay, load time and render delay -- turning "LCP is 3.8 s" into a specific thing to fix.
column3: frontend frontend-observability observability RUM errors tracing

column1: Why normalise route patterns before sending telemetry?
column2: Raw URLs with ids create unbounded cardinality, which is the usual cause of a telemetry bill tripling with no feature shipped, and it makes dashboards slow or unusable. Keep the raw URL as an unindexed attribute.
column3: frontend frontend-observability observability RUM errors tracing

column1: Why is the release identifier the most valuable field on an event?
column2: It enables error rate and p75 vitals per release, which is what turns a rollback decision from a debate into evidence -- and it is the signal automated canary analysis reads.
column3: frontend frontend-observability observability RUM errors tracing

column1: Sensible sampling rates by signal?
column2: Vitals 5-10% of sessions; errors 100% with fingerprint deduplication; resource timing 1-2%; custom business metrics 100%; session replay 0.1-1% biased toward error sessions; long tasks and profiles around 1%.
column3: frontend frontend-observability observability RUM errors tracing

column1: Why sample deterministically per session?
column2: So a sampled session sends all of its events and the story is coherent. Per-event sampling gives you fragments, and sampling by event rather than session biases toward long sessions.
column3: frontend frontend-observability observability RUM errors tracing

column1: Why must session-replay masking be default-deny?
column2: A denylist does not survive the next feature -- the engineer adding a field will not know it exists. Mask everything and explicitly unmask what you need; exclude credential and card fields entirely rather than masking them.
column3: frontend frontend-observability observability RUM errors tracing

column1: What does `traceparent` carry and what breaks when you add it?
column2: Version, a 32-hex trace id, a 16-hex parent span id, and flags whose low bit is the sampled flag. It is not CORS-safelisted, so cross-origin calls need it in `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` or the preflight fails.
column3: frontend frontend-observability observability RUM errors tracing

column1: Why alert on percentiles per cohort instead of global averages?
column2: A tripling of LCP for 8% of users barely moves a global mean and crosses no threshold. Alert on change against each cohort's own trailing baseline, with a minimum sample size so small cohorts do not page you on noise.
column3: frontend frontend-observability observability RUM errors tracing

column1: Why is a frontend deploy not a version replacement?
column2: You cannot take the old version out of service. Users hold builds in memory until they reload, so production always runs several versions at once and your compatibility window is roughly your p99 session duration.
column3: frontend deployment-and-rollout deployment canary migration flags

column1: Why must a deploy never delete old assets?
column2: Browsers hold HTML referencing the previous build's hashed chunks. Deleting them makes those dynamic imports 404, producing chunk-load errors and white screens -- often minutes later, on a lazily-loaded route. Retain 30 days.
column3: frontend deployment-and-rollout deployment canary migration flags

column1: The two-policy caching split for a deployable frontend?
column2: Hashed assets get `max-age=31536000, immutable`. HTML gets `max-age=0, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=600`, so deploys propagate in seconds and a bad deploy is a minute of exposure.
column3: frontend deployment-and-rollout deployment canary migration flags

column1: Why must canary bucketing be deterministic?
column2: Random per-request assignment gives a user HTML from one build and cached chunks from another. Hash a stable id, compare against the rollout percentage, and persist the result in a cookie set at the edge.
column3: frontend deployment-and-rollout deployment canary migration flags

column1: Which metrics make a canary gate actually work?
column2: Unhandled error rate per session, chunk-load error rate specifically, p75 INP and LCP for the cohort, and at least one funnel metric -- compared against concurrent baseline traffic with a minimum sample size.
column3: frontend deployment-and-rollout deployment canary migration flags

column1: What are the three phases of expand-migrate-contract?
column2: Expand: add the new thing alongside the old so every live version still works. Migrate: move readers and writers, backfill, and instrument old-path usage by client version. Contract: remove the old path once that usage has been zero longer than your compatibility window.
column3: frontend deployment-and-rollout deployment canary migration flags

column1: How do you safely kill an endpoint?
column2: Instrument per-caller usage, announce with `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers, then brownout -- return 410 for a minute at a quiet hour and see who complains -- before removing. Grepping the codebase misses callers you do not control.
column3: frontend deployment-and-rollout deployment canary migration flags

column1: Four flag types and their lifecycles?
column2: Release flags: temporary, 30-90 day expiry enforced by CI. Experiment flags: removed as part of the experiment's definition of done. Operational kill switches: permanent, but test the off path. Permission flags: not flags at all -- move them into the authorisation model.
column3: frontend deployment-and-rollout deployment canary migration flags

column1: What makes per-remote rollback possible in a federated frontend?
column2: Resolving remote versions from a short-TTL runtime manifest rather than hardcoding URLs in the host build, so rolling back one team's remote is a pointer flip that needs no rebuild and no shell deploy.
column3: frontend deployment-and-rollout deployment canary migration flags

column1: Why does an L4 load balancer create imbalance with HTTP/2 or gRPC?
column2: It balances once per TCP connection. HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests onto one long-lived connection, so a client is pinned to one backend for the connection's lifetime and new instances never receive its traffic.
column3: backend request-lifecycle load-balancing concurrency latency pooling

column1: Why does least-connections beat round robin under variable request cost?
column2: In-flight count is a free proxy for how busy a backend is. Round robin sends a cheap request to a node already stuck behind slow ones, creating queueing delay at the balancer. Least-connections routes around it.
column3: backend request-lifecycle load-balancing concurrency latency pooling

column1: What is the failure mode of least-connections?
column2: A backend failing fast has near-zero in-flight requests, so it looks idlest and attracts the most traffic. Pair it with outlier detection that ejects hosts on consecutive 5xx.
column3: backend request-lifecycle load-balancing concurrency latency pooling

column1: State Little's Law and apply it to a connection pool.
column2: `L = λ × W`. Busy connections equal query throughput times average query duration. At 2,400 queries/s and 4 ms each you need about 10 busy connections; size for p95 hold time, not p50.
column3: backend request-lifecycle load-balancing concurrency latency pooling

column1: Why does Postgres need pgBouncer while MySQL tolerates more connections?
column2: Postgres forks an OS process per connection, each with its own memory and a slot in snapshot computation, so throughput degrades past a few hundred. A transaction-mode pooler multiplexes hundreds of clients onto tens of server connections.
column3: backend request-lifecycle load-balancing concurrency latency pooling

column1: Why can a bigger connection pool make p99 worse?
column2: It moves queueing from your application into the database, where the wait is unbounded, unprioritised, invisible to your timeouts and not exposed as a metric.
column3: backend request-lifecycle load-balancing concurrency latency pooling

column1: What breaks when a CPU-bound handler runs on an event loop?
column2: It blocks every in-flight request on that instance, so latency rises uniformly across unrelated routes. Watch event-loop lag, not CPU, and move the work off the loop.
column3: backend request-lifecycle load-balancing concurrency latency pooling

column1: Why must virtual threads be paired with an explicit concurrency limit?
column2: The old thread pool was also the admission control. Virtual threads are effectively unbounded, so a slow dependency lets requests accumulate until the process dies of memory instead of shedding load. Reintroduce the bound with a semaphore or bulkhead.
column3: backend request-lifecycle load-balancing concurrency latency pooling

column1: Which single metric most often explains p99 that queries cannot?
column2: Connection acquisition wait time. Database instrumentation starts the clock when the query is sent, so time spent waiting for a pooled connection is invisible to it.
column3: backend request-lifecycle load-balancing concurrency latency pooling

column1: Why must an idempotency key be per-operation rather than per-attempt?
column2: The whole point is that the server recognises a retry of the same intent. A new key per attempt makes every retry a distinct operation, so a lost response becomes a duplicate write while the code looks correct.
column3: backend api-design-backend REST gRPC idempotency versioning

column1: How do you handle two concurrent retries with the same idempotency key?
column2: Claim the key with a unique-constrained insert. The loser sees state `in_flight` and returns `409` with `Retry-After` rather than executing; once the winner commits `completed`, subsequent calls replay the stored response.
column3: backend api-design-backend REST gRPC idempotency versioning

column1: Why hash the request body alongside the idempotency key?
column2: Same key with a different body is a client bug. Replaying the old response would hide it, so return `422 idempotency-key-reused` instead.
column3: backend api-design-backend REST gRPC idempotency versioning

column1: Why does `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000` get slow?
column2: The database reads and discards 100,000 rows to locate the window, so cost grows linearly with page depth. It is also unstable: concurrent inserts shift the offset and rows get skipped.
column3: backend api-design-backend REST gRPC idempotency versioning

column1: What two details make keyset pagination correct?
column2: A unique sort key -- compare a tuple like `(created_at, id)` so duplicate timestamps cannot repeat or drop rows -- and an opaque, ideally signed cursor so clients cannot construct one and you can change the sort key later.
column3: backend api-design-backend REST gRPC idempotency versioning

column1: Difference between a timeout and a deadline?
column2: A timeout is a per-hop duration and therefore multiplies down a call chain. A deadline is an absolute instant shared by the whole tree; each hop spends what remains minus its own reserve, so total time stays bounded.
column3: backend api-design-backend REST gRPC idempotency versioning

column1: What should `500` versus `503` versus `504` tell a client?
column2: `500` is an unexpected bug -- retry only if idempotent. `503` is temporary unavailability or shedding -- retry with backoff, honouring `Retry-After`. `504` is an upstream deadline -- the work may still be running, so retry cautiously.
column3: backend api-design-backend REST gRPC idempotency versioning

column1: Which protobuf changes are safe?
column2: Adding a field with a fresh tag, widening `int32` to `int64`, and removing a field *if* you `reserved` its tag and name. Changing a tag number, changing wire type, altering cardinality, or moving a field into a `oneof` are breaking.
column3: backend api-design-backend REST gRPC idempotency versioning

column1: Why does every protobuf enum need a zero value named `UNSPECIFIED`?
column2: Unknown enum values decode to the zero value in old readers. If zero is a real business meaning, a newly added value silently becomes that meaning; if zero is `UNSPECIFIED`, the client can detect and log it.
column3: backend api-design-backend REST gRPC idempotency versioning

column1: Why is a B+tree lookup fast even on a 100 million row table?
column2: Fan-out of ~300 per 8 KB page means four levels address billions of entries, and the upper levels stay cached. A point lookup is one or two real disk reads regardless of table size.
column3: backend databases-and-indexes indexes B-tree query-plan Postgres

column1: State the leftmost-prefix rule.
column2: An index on `(a, b, c)` can seek on `a`, `(a, b)`, or `(a, b, c)` -- any leftmost prefix. It cannot seek on `b` alone, because `b` values are scattered across every value of `a`.
column3: backend databases-and-indexes indexes B-tree query-plan Postgres

column1: Where does a range predicate belong in a composite index, and why?
column2: Last. A range consumes the rest of the index because columns after it are not globally ordered within the range, so they degrade to row-by-row filters.
column3: backend databases-and-indexes indexes B-tree query-plan Postgres

column1: What is an index-only scan, and what can silently break it in Postgres?
column2: The query is answered from index leaves with no heap access. It requires pages marked all-visible in the visibility map, so when autovacuum falls behind, `Heap Fetches` becomes non-zero and the plan quietly gets slower.
column3: backend databases-and-indexes indexes B-tree query-plan Postgres

column1: When is the planner right to choose a sequential scan?
column2: When selectivity is poor -- roughly above 5-10% of the table. Sequential I/O is about an order of magnitude cheaper per page than random heap fetches, so scanning beats looking up most of a table.
column3: backend databases-and-indexes indexes B-tree query-plan Postgres

column1: What is a bitmap heap scan and when does Postgres use it?
column2: It collects matching row pointers from an index, sorts them by physical page, then reads each page once. It is chosen at medium selectivity -- too many rows for per-row random fetches, too few for a full scan.
column3: backend databases-and-indexes indexes B-tree query-plan Postgres

column1: Why is a UUIDv4 primary key bad in InnoDB?
column2: Rows live inside the clustered PK tree, so random keys cause page splits and fragmentation on insert, and every secondary index stores the 16-byte PK as its pointer. A monotonic bigint or UUIDv7 avoids the insert problem.
column3: backend databases-and-indexes indexes B-tree query-plan Postgres

column1: Give the write cost of an index in Postgres specifically.
column2: A non-HOT update writes a new tuple version and must add an entry to every index on the table, even for unindexed columns. That multiplies WAL sent to disk, replicas and backups. `fillfactor` enables HOT updates when no indexed column changed.
column3: backend databases-and-indexes indexes B-tree query-plan Postgres

column1: Why is an N+1 query pattern hard to spot in database metrics?
column2: Each individual query is fast and well indexed, so nothing appears in slow-query logs. It shows up only as queries-per-request in a trace, and its cost scales linearly with page size.
column3: backend databases-and-indexes indexes B-tree query-plan Postgres

column1: What does the C in ACID actually guarantee?
column2: Only that constraints you declared -- keys, checks, foreign keys -- hold at commit. A business invariant such as "balance never goes negative" is protected only if it is an actual `CHECK` constraint.
column3: backend transactions-and-isolation ACID MVCC isolation locking

column1: Explain MVCC visibility in Postgres via xmin and xmax.
column2: Each tuple records the creating transaction (`xmin`) and the deleting/superseding one (`xmax`). A snapshot sees a tuple if `xmin` committed before the snapshot and `xmax` is unset or uncommitted. Readers and writers therefore never block each other.
column3: backend transactions-and-isolation ACID MVCC isolation locking

column1: Why can one idle transaction bloat your whole database?
column2: Vacuum can only remove a tuple version once no live snapshot could need it. An old snapshot pins that horizon cluster-wide, so dead tuples accumulate on tables the session never touched, and index-only scans degrade as the visibility map goes stale.
column3: backend transactions-and-isolation ACID MVCC isolation locking

column1: What is write skew, and why does snapshot isolation permit it?
column2: Two transactions read the same set, then write *different* rows, jointly breaking an invariant. No transaction writes a row the other read, so there is no version conflict to detect -- only Serializable tracks predicate conflicts.
column3: backend transactions-and-isolation ACID MVCC isolation locking

column1: Three ways to defend against write skew?
column2: Run Serializable and retry `40001`; materialise the conflict by locking a row that represents the invariant; or encode the invariant as a unique or check constraint so it holds regardless of isolation level.
column3: backend transactions-and-isolation ACID MVCC isolation locking

column1: How does Postgres Repeatable Read differ from MySQL InnoDB Repeatable Read?
column2: Postgres raises `40001` if you update a row changed since your snapshot. MySQL lets locking reads (`FOR UPDATE`, and the internal reads of `UPDATE`/`DELETE`) see the latest committed row instead of your snapshot, mixing two points in time silently. MySQL also uses gap locks to block phantoms.
column3: backend transactions-and-isolation ACID MVCC isolation locking

column1: What is SSI and what does it demand from the application?
column2: Serializable Snapshot Isolation detects dangerous read/write dependency structures using non-blocking predicate locks and aborts one transaction with `40001`. The application must retry the entire transaction with jitter; aborts are the mechanism, not a bug.
column3: backend transactions-and-isolation ACID MVCC isolation locking

column1: When is optimistic concurrency better than `SELECT FOR UPDATE`?
column2: When conflicts are rare and the decision takes a long time -- a user editing a form. No lock is held while thinking. It degrades under high contention, where a bounded pessimistic lock is better.
column3: backend transactions-and-isolation ACID MVCC isolation locking

column1: What removes a whole class of deadlocks?
column2: Consistent lock ordering -- acquire rows in a deterministic total order, e.g. `WHERE id IN (...) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE`, so two transactions can never hold locks the other needs in the opposite order.
column3: backend transactions-and-isolation ACID MVCC isolation locking

column1: What is the first artefact of a data-modelling exercise?
column2: An access-pattern inventory: each read and write with its rate, latency target and consistency requirement. The ratios in that table determine whether you can afford fan-out-on-write, denormalised counters, or a separate search store.
column3: backend data-modeling modelling NoSQL DynamoDB schema

column1: Why does DynamoDB push you toward single-table design?
column2: It offers one efficient primitive -- fetch items by partition key, narrowed and sorted by sort key. With no joins and no efficient non-key filters, the only way to serve a pattern in one round trip is to co-locate heterogeneous item types under a shared partition key.
column3: backend data-modeling modelling NoSQL DynamoDB schema

column1: Why encode status in a DynamoDB sort key rather than as an attribute?
column2: `FilterExpression` is applied after items are read, so you pay for every item in the partition. `begins_with(SK, 'TASK#OPEN#')` reads only matching items. The cost is that changing status means delete-and-insert, since key attributes are immutable.
column3: backend data-modeling modelling NoSQL DynamoDB schema

column1: What is a sparse GSI and why is it useful?
column2: Only items carrying the index key attributes are projected into it. Adding `GSI1PK` to task items alone gives you an index containing tasks and nothing else, so you pay storage and write cost only for those items.
column3: backend data-modeling modelling NoSQL DynamoDB schema

column1: Distinguish denormalisation from temporal snapshotting.
column2: Denormalisation copies a live shared fact (display name on posts) and needs a fan-out job plus a reconciler. A temporal snapshot records a fact as of an instant (price at purchase) and must *never* be updated -- it is not a duplicate at all.
column3: backend data-modeling modelling NoSQL DynamoDB schema

column1: What single rule keeps denormalisation survivable?
column2: Exactly one source of truth, and every derived copy must be rebuildable from it by a batch job. Then a fan-out bug is an inconvenience rather than permanent data loss.
column3: backend data-modeling modelling NoSQL DynamoDB schema

column1: When is `jsonb` the wrong choice?
column2: As soon as a query filters on a value inside it or code branches on it. You lose type checking, `NOT NULL`, foreign keys and good selectivity estimates, and you need an expression or GIN index per access path.
column3: backend data-modeling modelling NoSQL DynamoDB schema

column1: Why are columnar stores 10-100x faster for analytics?
column2: Each column is stored contiguously, so a query referencing 3 of 60 columns reads only those bytes, and per-column uniformity gives 5-20x compression. The trade is that reconstructing a single whole row requires many separate column reads.
column3: backend data-modeling modelling NoSQL DynamoDB schema

column1: When does a graph database beat a recursive CTE?
column2: When traversal depth is variable and unknown at query time -- shortest path, unbounded permission inheritance -- and traversal is a core product feature. Depth-2 questions are two joins, and bounded hierarchies are a depth-capped, cycle-safe recursive CTE.
column3: backend data-modeling modelling NoSQL DynamoDB schema

column1: Why is the difference between a 95% and 90% hit rate so significant?
column2: It doubles origin load. At 50,000 rps total, 95% leaves 2,500 rps on the database and 90% leaves 5,000. The cache is sized to make the database survivable, so hit rate directly determines whether it does.
column3: backend server-side-caching Redis cache-aside stampede eviction

column1: Describe cache stampede and the three composable defences.
column2: At TTL expiry every concurrent request for a hot key misses and runs the expensive load at once. Defend with in-process request coalescing, a `SET NX` rebuild lock across instances, and a soft/hard TTL so a stale copy is served while one caller rebuilds. Jitter TTLs so keys do not expire together.
column3: backend server-side-caching Redis cache-aside stampede eviction

column1: What is probabilistic early expiry?
column2: Each reader refreshes with a probability rising near expiry, weighted by measured recompute cost -- `now - delta * beta * ln(random()) >= expiry`. It spreads refreshes across the window with no locks or coordination, and refreshes expensive keys earlier.
column3: backend server-side-caching Redis cache-aside stampede eviction

column1: Why can you not scale a hot Redis key by adding nodes?
column2: A key hashes to exactly one of 16,384 slots, owned by one node, executing commands on one thread -- roughly 100,000 ops/s. Mitigate with a short-TTL local cache in front, key replication across suffixes, or client-side caching.
