column1: What are the five span kinds in an LLM trace?
column2: Retrieval, model call, tool call, guardrail, and an agent-step span that parents the others inside a loop. Nesting matters because the useful questions are about relationships between spans -- did the retrieval that preceded this generation contain the answer?
column3: ai ai-observability tracing OpenTelemetry cost feedback

column1: Why record requested and resolved model separately?
column2: `gen_ai.request.model` may be a floating alias; `gen_ai.response.model` is the snapshot that actually served you. When behaviour shifts with no deploy, grouping by resolved model finds a silent provider swap immediately.
column3: ai ai-observability tracing OpenTelemetry cost feedback

column1: What must never go into exported telemetry?
column2: Credentials and secrets at any sampling rate, and un-redacted PII from prompts or retrieved chunks. Redact before export, keep payloads in your own store with short retention, and gate raw payload access behind a separate audited permission.
column3: ai ai-observability tracing OpenTelemetry cost feedback

column1: Why is tail sampling right for payloads?
column2: Payloads exist for debugging, and debugging is about outliers. Tail sampling decides after the trace completes, so you can keep 100% of errors, outlier-cost runs, latency breaches and negative feedback. Head sampling discards exactly the traces you get paged about.
column3: ai ai-observability tracing OpenTelemetry cost feedback

column1: Why are thumbs-up/down weak, and what replaces them?
column2: Single-digit response rates with selection bias toward the delighted and furious, so the ratio describes your sampling. Use implicit signals joined on trace ID: edit survival, regenerate rate, rephrase-and-ask-again, abandonment point, escalation.
column3: ai ai-observability tracing OpenTelemetry cost feedback

column1: What do you need to replay a failed run?
column2: Exact serialised messages, prompt template version, resolved model snapshot and sampling parameters, tool schema version, and raw tool responses. Cached replay isolates your own logic; live replay tells you whether the world drifted.
column3: ai ai-observability tracing OpenTelemetry cost feedback

column1: Which AI-specific signals deserve alerts?
column2: Retrieval-empty rate, schema/parse failure rate, refusal-rate deviation in either direction, p95 TTFT separately from total, cache hit rate, cost-per-request rate of change, truncation on `finish_reason=length`, and escalation/regenerate rate.
column3: ai ai-observability tracing OpenTelemetry cost feedback

column1: Why is a drop in refusal rate also worth alerting on?
column2: Refusals are a feature. A sudden drop can mean a guardrail stopped firing, a safety filter was misconfigured, or a prompt change removed a constraint -- so alert on deviation in either direction, not just increases.
column3: ai ai-observability tracing OpenTelemetry cost feedback

column1: Why are prefill and decode fundamentally different workloads?
column2: Prefill processes all input tokens in one parallel pass and is compute-bound. Decode produces one token per pass, sequentially, and is memory-bandwidth-bound because each pass reads the whole weight matrix. Prefill governs TTFT, decode governs inter-token latency.
column3: ai inference-serving vLLM KV-cache batching quantisation

column1: Write the KV cache size formula.
column2: 2 (K and V) x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes_per_element x sequence_length. For 80 layers, 8 KV heads, head dim 128, BF16: about 0.31 MiB per token, so an 8k-token request is roughly 2.5 GiB.
column3: ai inference-serving vLLM KV-cache batching quantisation

column1: What did PagedAttention actually fix, and what was the bigger win?
column2: It replaced contiguous per-request KV allocation sized for max output -- which wasted most of the cache on reservations -- with fixed 16-token blocks and a block table. The bigger win is that blocks became *shareable*, which is the mechanism underneath prefix caching and cheap parallel sampling.
column3: ai inference-serving vLLM KV-cache batching quantisation

column1: Why does continuous batching beat static batching?
column2: Static batching runs until the longest sequence finishes, leaving completed slots idle. Continuous batching evicts finished sequences and admits queued ones every iteration, so the GPU never waits for a straggler. The win grows with output-length variance.
column3: ai inference-serving vLLM KV-cache batching quantisation

column1: What does `max_num_batched_tokens` trade off?
column2: It is the prefill token budget per scheduler step. Smaller (around 2,048) gives better ITL because prefills interrupt decode less; larger (8,192+) gives better TTFT and throughput. It is the clearest single expression of the latency-throughput frontier.
column3: ai inference-serving vLLM KV-cache batching quantisation

column1: When does speculative decoding hurt?
column2: Under saturation. Verification compute competes with other requests’ real tokens, so total throughput can fall even as single-request latency improves. It is a latency optimisation for low-to-moderate load, and its value scales with draft acceptance rate.
column3: ai inference-serving vLLM KV-cache batching quantisation

column1: Weight-only versus weight-and-activation quantisation?
column2: Weight-only (W4A16, W8A16) shrinks stored weights and dequantises to compute in higher precision -- directly attacks the decode bottleneck with modest quality risk. Weight-and-activation (FP8 W8A8, W4A8) also narrows activations so the matmuls run in low precision: faster, riskier, needs calibration.
column3: ai inference-serving vLLM KV-cache batching quantisation

column1: Tensor versus pipeline parallelism?
column2: Tensor parallelism shards each layer across GPUs, cutting memory *and* latency but paying an all-reduce per layer -- needs NVLink-class interconnect, use within a node. Pipeline parallelism assigns whole layers to GPUs with small communication but adds latency and bubbles -- use it to make a model fit across nodes, not to go faster.
column3: ai inference-serving vLLM KV-cache batching quantisation

column1: What should you autoscale an inference tier on?
column2: Queue depth and time-in-queue, with KV cache utilisation and preemption rate as secondary signals. Never GPU utilisation -- batched decode reads as busy whether or not anyone is waiting, so it never triggers scale-up while TTFT breaches.
column3: ai inference-serving vLLM KV-cache batching quantisation

column1: Where does AI spend actually go?
column2: Mostly input tokens -- system prompt, tool schemas, retrieved context and history, all re-sent every call, and re-sent every step in an agent loop. Retries and abandoned runs are usually the second largest and least tracked line.
column3: ai model-routing-and-cost routing cost caching failover

column1: Why is prefix caching the highest-leverage cost lever?
column2: It cuts input-token price substantially (discounts around 90% are common) *and* reduces TTFT, with zero quality cost. Nothing else improves cost and latency at the same time.
column3: ai model-routing-and-cost routing cost caching failover

column1: What breaks prefix caching?
column2: Any token change near the start, because matching is prefix-exact. Timestamps, user names or request IDs at the top of the system prompt, and non-deterministically ordered retrieved chunks. Order prompts stable-first, volatile-last, and alert on cache hit rate.
column3: ai model-routing-and-cost routing cost caching failover

column1: What makes a good cascade escalation signal?
column2: A deterministic verification failure -- output did not parse, schema invalid, citation IDs do not resolve, SQL did not execute, tests failed. Then explicit `INSUFFICIENT_CONTEXT` style self-assessment, then log-prob signals, then a classifier trained on your own escalation labels.
column3: ai model-routing-and-cost routing cost caching failover

column1: When does a cascade stop paying?
column2: When escalation is common. At a 10x tier price gap, escalating 20% of traffic still saves roughly 70%; escalating 60% saves almost nothing once you count the wasted first call. Monitor escalation rate and treat a rise as a quality regression.
column3: ai model-routing-and-cost routing cost caching failover

column1: Why is semantic caching dangerous?
column2: Similar questions can have different answers -- qualifiers and negations especially, since embeddings handle negation poorly. And without tenant plus permission scope in the key it leaks data across tenants, the same failure class as caching personalised HTML in a shared CDN.
column3: ai model-routing-and-cost routing cost caching failover

column1: How should a tenant budget be enforced and what happens at the limit?
column2: A shared atomic counter in the gateway, never per process, or the effective cap multiplies by replica count. Degrade in stages: notify at ~70%, cheap tier and lower k at ~85%, cache-only plus deferral at 100%, then a clear message naming the reset time and an upgrade path.
column3: ai model-routing-and-cost routing cost caching failover

column1: Why is retrieval-k both a cost and a quality dial?
column2: k drives the largest volatile part of the prompt, so k=20 to k=5 cuts that component about 4x -- and quality often improves, because long contexts lose the middle and irrelevant chunks distract. Plot eval score against k and take the knee.
column3: ai model-routing-and-cost routing cost caching failover

column1: What is the honest caveat about multi-provider failover?
column2: The API surface is portable; the prompts are not. Models differ in instruction following, tool-call syntax, refusal boundaries, long-context behaviour and tokenisation. Treat failover as a declared capability tier with a tuned, eval-gated prompt variant per model.
column3: ai model-routing-and-cost routing cost caching failover

column1: The one-line rule for fine-tuning versus retrieval?
column2: Fine-tuning teaches form and behaviour; retrieval supplies facts. If the requirement involves citations, freshness or per-document permissions, it is a retrieval requirement and weights are the wrong place for it.
column3: ai finetuning-and-adaptation fine-tuning LoRA DPO distillation

column1: What does SFT mechanically change?
column2: Next-token prediction on your examples, with loss usually masked to the response tokens. It shifts the probability distribution over continuations so outputs look like your responses -- excellent for structure, tone and schema, poor for facts.
column3: ai finetuning-and-adaptation fine-tuning LoRA DPO distillation

column1: How does LoRA work, and what does the parameter count look like?
column2: Freeze W, learn A (r x k) and B (d x r), effective weight W + (alpha/r)·BA. For an 8192x8192 projection at r=16 that is about 260k trainable parameters instead of 67M -- roughly 0.4% for that matrix, and 0.05-0.5% across a whole model.
column3: ai finetuning-and-adaptation fine-tuning LoRA DPO distillation

column1: What do rank and alpha control?
column2: Rank r is adapter capacity: 4-8 for style, 16-32 as the common default for task specialisation, 64+ rarely worth the overfitting risk. Alpha scales the adapter contribution; the alpha/r ratio is what matters, not either value alone.
column3: ai finetuning-and-adaptation fine-tuning LoRA DPO distillation

column1: Why does QLoRA make large-model fine-tuning affordable?
column2: The base weights are quantised to 4-bit and frozen, and only the higher-precision adapters are trained. Since the base is never updated, quantising it costs much less than quantising a model you intend to train fully -- a 70B LoRA then fits on one 80 GB GPU.

column1: DPO versus RLHF, and when to use either?
column2: RLHF trains a reward model then optimises with RL -- powerful, complex, prone to reward hacking. DPO gets a similar objective in closed form from preferred/rejected pairs with a KL anchor, and is now the default. Use either *after* SFT, and only for taste you cannot demonstrate.
column3: ai finetuning-and-adaptation fine-tuning LoRA DPO distillation

column1: Why is distillation the most common production win?
column2: You have an oracle. The hard part of fine-tuning is the dataset, and a teacher generates unlimited labelled data on your real input distribution with a measurable quality target -- typically yielding ~10x lower cost and much lower latency on a narrow task.
column3: ai finetuning-and-adaptation fine-tuning LoRA DPO distillation

column1: How do you detect capability regression after fine-tuning?
column2: Run the full eval suite plus a standing regression set of capabilities the fine-tune was never meant to touch -- instruction following, tool-call formatting, refusal behaviour, unrelated task types. Watch validation loss, use 1-3 epochs, load the best checkpoint not the last.
column3: ai finetuning-and-adaptation fine-tuning LoRA DPO distillation

column1: What is the maintenance cost of a fine-tune?
column2: Adapters are specific to a base architecture and checkpoint, so a base deprecation forces re-training, re-evaluation and re-qualification. Meanwhile a general model two generations newer with a good prompt may match your fine-tune for free.

column1: Why is prompt injection not fixable the way SQL injection was?
column2: Prepared statements work by putting instructions and data in different channels. A transformer has one token channel -- system prompt, user message, retrieved text and tool results are all one sequence -- so role markers are learned convention, not a structural boundary. There is no prepared-statement equivalent.
column3: ai ai-security prompt-injection guardrails PII authorisation

column1: Direct versus indirect injection?
column2: Direct: the user attacks through their own input, so the blast radius is their own session -- treat your system prompt as public. Indirect: an attacker plants instructions in content your system later retrieves, so the victim is a different user and the payload arrives through a trusted path. Indirect is the serious one.
column3: ai ai-security prompt-injection guardrails PII authorisation

column1: What is the lethal trifecta, and how do you use it?
column2: Private data access + exposure to untrusted content + a way to communicate externally. All three and assume exfiltration is possible; remove any one and the attack cannot complete. Decide which leg to break *per capability* rather than accepting the combination globally.
column3: ai ai-security prompt-injection guardrails PII authorisation

column1: Why are injection classifiers mitigation rather than prevention?
column2: A probabilistic classifier facing an adaptive adversary with unlimited attempts across all of natural language plus every encoding. At realistic base rates, 95% recall still passes one attack in twenty while producing enough false positives that someone disables it. Use them for depth and telemetry.
column3: ai ai-security prompt-injection guardrails PII authorisation

column1: What is wrong with giving the AI service a broad service account?
column2: It makes the model’s authority the union of every user’s authority, so one successful injection escalates to a system-wide breach -- the confused deputy in pure form. Propagate the end user’s identity via short-lived scoped credentials so downstream services authorise normally.
column3: ai ai-security prompt-injection guardrails PII authorisation

column1: Why must ACL filters be applied inside the retrieval query?
column2: Post-filtering means unauthorised content was already retrieved into your process and probably your logs, and removing results afterwards makes effective k unpredictable. Store permissions with the vectors, filter in the query, and propagate upstream permission changes into the index.
column3: ai ai-security prompt-injection guardrails PII authorisation

column1: Name the main exfiltration channels.
column2: Rendered markdown images (zero-click), links, any HTTP tool the model can aim, email/message/webhook sends, DNS lookups with data in the subdomain, and writes to any store the attacker can read. A default-deny egress allowlist is the backstop for the one you missed.
column3: ai ai-security prompt-injection guardrails PII authorisation

column1: What is the rule for model output?
column2: Treat it exactly as untrusted user input. Never `innerHTML`, never `eval`/`exec`/shell, never interpolated into SQL, never a file path without canonicalisation, never a server-side fetch URL without an allowlist.
column3: ai ai-security prompt-injection guardrails PII authorisation

column1: Why is an MCP server a prompt-injection surface, and what belongs in the audit log?
column2: An MCP server supplies the tool names, descriptions and parameter docs that go directly into your model’s context, so a compromised or silently updated server can instruct exfiltration and your own prompt cannot defend against it -- pin, review, vendor the definitions, and alert on description changes. Separately, audit every action with run ID, end user, resolved model and prompt version, redacted tool args, outcome and approver: append-only and retained longer than payloads, because "what did it touch and on whose behalf?" must be answerable in minutes.
column3: ai ai-security prompt-injection guardrails PII authorisation

column1: Why is TTFT the metric AI UX is designed around?
column2: Perceived latency is dominated by the silence before anything appears; once tokens stream the user is reading and the clock feels slower. TTFT is also the part you control — prompt size, prefix cache hits, and whether you do a retrieval round trip first.
column3: ai ai-product-ux streaming UX trust feedback

column1: Why does raising decode throughput above ~8 tokens/sec stop helping?
column2: That is roughly human reading speed. Above it the user is never waiting on generation in a streaming interface, so extra tokens per second are imperceptible. Spend the effort on TTFT, quality, or a cheaper model instead.
column3: ai ai-product-ux streaming UX trust feedback

column1: What should you show before the first token?
column2: The real work, named: "Searching your documents", then the source titles as they resolve, then "Writing answer". It converts dead time into a progress narrative, sets expectations about what the answer is based on, and lets the user cancel early if the sources are obviously wrong.
column3: ai ai-product-ux streaming UX trust feedback

column1: Why is generic hedging worse than no hedging?
column2: A constant disclaimer carries no information — it cannot distinguish a well-grounded answer from a shaky one — and it trains users to ignore all warnings including the ones that mattered. Differentiate using real signals: retrieval scores, source agreement, and scope.
column3: ai ai-product-ux streaming UX trust feedback

column1: Why are citations the primary trust mechanism?
column2: They make verification cheap and local: the user checks one claim in two seconds instead of evaluating the whole answer. Link to anchors with hover previews, resolve IDs to URLs in your own code, and verify every cited ID exists — a fabricated citation makes a wrong answer more dangerous than an uncited one.
column3: ai ai-product-ux streaming UX trust feedback

column1: What is the "stage then commit" pattern?
column2: The model produces a proposal — a diff, a draft, a pull request — which the user reviews, edits and explicitly applies. It turns a binary accept/reject into collaboration, and it keeps the irreversible action with a human who has the authority to take it.
column3: ai ai-product-ux streaming UX trust feedback

column1: Why are thumbs up/down a weak feedback signal?
column2: Low response rate, biased toward the angry and the delighted, ambiguous meaning, and gameable — optimising against them rewards agreeableness over accuracy. Use edits, accept rates, regenerations, abandonment and escalations instead, all attributed to a trace ID.
column3: ai ai-product-ux streaming UX trust feedback

column1: What should happen when a stream dies mid-answer?
column2: Persist what arrived, mark it clearly incomplete, and offer to continue from that point. Users forgive an incomplete answer and do not forgive losing one they were reading. Stream resumption should be keyed by generation ID.
column3: ai ai-product-ux streaming UX trust feedback

column1: What are the tiers of graceful degradation for a provider outage?
column2: Retry with backoff and jitter, fail over to a secondary provider or smaller model with a quality note, serve a cached answer for a repeated question, then fall back to the deterministic non-AI path — keyword search, docs link, human handoff. The last tier is the one teams skip and the one that keeps the product usable.
column3: ai ai-product-ux streaming UX trust feedback

column1: Why is a gateway non-negotiable at org scale?
column2: Auth, tenant resolution, quota, residency policy, PII redaction, retries, telemetry and audit are cross-cutting and correctness-critical. A control implemented per application is one the next team will forget -- and a gateway 60% of traffic bypasses provides 0% of the governance.
column3: ai ai-platform-architecture platform gateway multi-tenant governance

column1: What is the first deliverable of an AI platform, and why?
column2: A transparent OpenAI-compatible proxy doing auth, tenant tagging, telemetry, cost attribution and retries -- nothing opinionated. Migration costs a base URL and a key, and you get 100% visibility before adding any restriction. Visibility, then control, then optimisation.
column3: ai ai-platform-architecture platform gateway multi-tenant governance

column1: Build versus buy, in one rule?
column2: Build what encodes your tenancy, policy, rollout and pricing model -- gateway policy layer, registry, cost attribution, eval datasets. Buy translation and commodity infrastructure -- provider adapters, tracing backends, eval runners, indexes, sandboxes. Never write a serving engine.
column3: ai ai-platform-architecture platform gateway multi-tenant governance

column1: Why must routing be configuration rather than code?
column2: So a model deprecation is a one-day config change with a staged rollout and eval gate, not an eight-team coordination project. The gateway should refuse raw provider model names and accept only logical names the registry resolves.
column3: ai ai-platform-architecture platform gateway multi-tenant governance

column1: What three properties does a prompt registry need?
column2: Immutable versioning, so a trace recording v17 can be replayed exactly; staged rollout with a canary percentage, because a prompt change is a production change; and eval gating on promotion, which wires the eval plane into the deployment path.
column3: ai ai-platform-architecture platform gateway multi-tenant governance

column1: How do you isolate tenants in shared retrieval?
column2: Tiered: namespaces for the long tail with ACL filters applied inside the query through one shared query-builder applications cannot bypass, dedicated indexes for large enterprise tenants, separate infrastructure where contracts require it -- plus a continuous job verifying retrieved doc IDs against caller entitlements.
column3: ai ai-platform-architecture platform gateway multi-tenant governance

column1: Who owns prompts and eval datasets?
column2: Product teams. They require domain knowledge the platform team does not have, and centralising authorship creates a queue and produces worse prompts. Platform owns the mechanism and defaults; security and legal own the model-and-data-class catalogue, not per-feature review.
column3: ai ai-platform-architecture platform gateway multi-tenant governance

column1: How do you keep AI governance from becoming a bottleneck?
column2: Risk-tier it. Internal, read-only, human-in-the-loop, no-PII features self-serve against automated CI checks. Reserve human review for customer-facing autonomous action, regulated workflows, new data classes and new providers. Approval is a catalogue entry, not a meeting.
column3: ai ai-platform-architecture platform gateway multi-tenant governance

column1: Name four ways the platform itself fails, and would you start with showback or chargeback?
column2: Gateway as SPOF (stateless multi-region, cached policy with stale-if-error, fail-open telemetry, audited break-glass); noisy neighbour (per-tenant quotas, separate batch queue class); version skew (versioned API, contract tests, consumer version on every span); platform-as-bottleneck (self-serve tiers plus a documented escape hatch). Start with showback -- most of the behavioural benefit, far less friction, and time to reconcile attribution against provider invoices before anyone’s budget depends on your numbers.
